verdict.text:
A caveat first. The study context says non-atomic requirements were excluded, but this run is the blind task on 50 source requests, and gold expects 77 units. Fifteen of those requests are non-atomic in gold (tp+fn). Either the wrong dataset was fed in, or the context note does not apply to this run. That needs resolving before anything here goes into the report. The analysis below describes the data as given.

Track 1 is measurable for scope (76 gold-missing) and condition (35), and the result is poor. Haiku zero-shot flagged only 12 of 76 missing scopes and 7 of 35 missing conditions. The real picture is worse, because 4 of the 12 scope "detections" are not detections at all. They are units that received an empty conversion after under-splitting: 6390-Signal#2, 222-Signal#1, 222-Signal#2 and 7567-Signal#1. Those score as all-missing by default. The genuine scope flag rate is closer to 8 of 72, about 11%.

The dominant behaviour is to invent a scope phrase for almost every requirement, even though the annotators uniformly wrote `<MISSING_SCOPE>`. This is the fabrication risk the experiment probes, and it is systematic rather than occasional. Actor and modalVerb have one gold-missing case each and action has four, so their F1 values carry no information. Their false positives come mostly from the empty units and from 1504-Signal and 592-Signal.

The 0.95 overall-verdict agreement is misleading and should not be quoted as a success. It mostly reflects both sides calling the core triple (actor, modal, action) present.

Title-only requests expose genuine ambiguity. In 83-Signal the model wrote "The System shall `<MISSING_ACTION>`", inventing an actor and declining the action. In 496-Signal it did roughly the reverse. The annotators themselves split on 83-Signal, so these cases are partly a gold-standard problem.

Decomposition is erratic. Non-atomic recall is decent at 0.8, but precision is 0.48, and the model returned 152 units against 77 expected. The extreme cases are 316-Signal (1→18), 1504-Signal (1→13), 4821-Signal (2→14) and 328-Signal (5→18), which suggests it is converting every sentence of long issue bodies, bug-report boilerplate included. It also under-split three requests (222, 6390, 7567), producing the empty units above.

Similarity is about 72% of the human ceiling on sequence ratio (0.52 vs 0.72) and 61% on Jaccard (0.34 vs 0.55). Removing the four zero-score empty units only lifts the LLM mean to about 0.55. With 231 pairs and a standard deviation near 0.2, a gap of roughly 0.2 is well outside noise. The conversions are substantially further from the humans than the humans are from each other. The cosine figures (n=12, all zero) look like a pipeline bug and should be ignored.

The Paska pass rate of 74% looks respectable, but Paska does not penalise fabricated scope, so it is blind to the main failure. Its smells concentrate on passive voice in conditions (10) and condition-after-response ordering (3). Three outputs that were kept as single units still carried more than one action (6457-Signal, 222-Signal#3, 1065-Signal#1). This shows the model both over-splits and under-splits within the same run.

Next steps, in order. First, reconcile the dataset with the atomic-only claim. Second, inspect the raw outputs to see what the invented scopes actually say. Third, add an explicit instruction to emit `<MISSING_SCOPE>` and `<MISSING_CONDITION>` unless the source states them, and rerun. Fourth, change the scorer so unaligned or empty units are reported separately rather than counted as correct missing-flags.

This is a single zero-shot run on 50 requests, so the comparison with few-shot and chain-of-thought will matter more than any absolute number here.
